To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dark matter mass can be determined, but not its spin, the scalar coupling or the inelastic parameter.

(1) the next generation of multi-target direct detection facilities can measure the sign of the scalar couplings and the ratio of the axial couplings; (2) the next generation cannot constrain the scalar-proton couplings; (3) only the dark matter particle mass and the inelasticy parameter can be inferred from the direct detection data.

(i) a multi-target signal is needed to constrain the dark matter parameter-space, (ii) the scalar-proton couplings cannot be measured, (iii) a combination of sodium-iodine targets will allow for a measurement of the axial-proton couplings, (iv) the elastic/inelastic nature of the interaction can be determined, and (v) the dark matter mass may be measured, but only with the help of additional information.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the limitations of direct dark matter searches and the implications of these for the interpretation of the data.
a careful assessment of the information that can be extracted from future direct dark matter experiments and the conclusions we draw are of general interest in this context.
the question: what can (not) be learned from future direct detection experiments?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the next generation of direct detection facilities will be able to measure the dark matter mass, the inelastic parameter, the axial-proton couplings and the ratio of scalar to axial couplings, but not the absolute scale of the scalar couplings.
the next generation of multi-ton direct detection facilities will be able to determine whether dark matter interacts with the Standard Model, but will not be able to determine its properties.

a multi-target, multi-ton experiment will be able to determine the dark matter mass, the inelastic parameter and the ratio of scalar and axial couplings to protons, but not the absolute values of the scalar and axial cross-sections.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while the scalar-proton coupling will remain essentially unconstrained, the axial-proton coupling can be determined with high accuracy, and both the dark matter mass as well as the inelastic parameter will be measurable with good accuracy as well.

the next generation of dark matter experiments will provide us with the first hints of what the WIMP really looks like, but the full answer to this question will require a multi-pronged approach involving complementary probes.
the next generation of direct searches for dark matter will be able to measure a number of quantities, including the WIMP mass, but will not be able to measure the WIMP-proton cross-section.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the dark matter mass can be measured with a high precision, the interpretation of the data in terms of the dark matter properties is far from being unique.

, while a multi-target approach can provide a more robust and accurate determination of the dark matter properties, the prospects for a discovery in the next generation of experiments are rather limited.
a multi-target strategy is crucial for the next generation of experiments, as it can help to disentangle the different dark matter couplings and, ultimately, unveil the underlying dark matter model.
